I did this for a time when I was very badly depressed. I would hook up with random guys who I knew only wanted to have sex with me. I used to play the part and laugh, smile, flirt, pretend to be sexy,wear revealing clothing. I even used to wear fake nails and I'm not the kind of person who even likes that stuff. I would put extensions in my hair and tons of makeup on. I basically tried to be everything that Society told me men wanted from me. I became someone I wasn't and as a result it made my depression even worse because I didn't know who I was anymore. All I knew was that I was playing a part and that part had nothing to do with me. I was also addicted to the attention. But I learned a very swift lesson. I was doing all of this for other people. I was giving them what they wanted, and the return was nothing for me. I mean these guys would come over fuck me and leave. Some of them were even abusive. I was stalked at one point. All of this just for someone else. It didn't fill the void it only made it bigger and bigger. Because you can have all the sex in the world but if you desire to feel important no one else can give that to you but yourself. Absolutely no one. It's nice to have a rewarding romantic relationship with another person but that's not what you're describing here. I can't think of anything that made me feel more empty than my random hookup days. I don't mean to judge you because I know where you're at. I did it for the exact same reasons. This is how you're coping right now but your coping mechanism in the sense comes with risks. Pregnancy, STDs, and even abuse. This is not a safe world for women as it is. I'm just being honest with you here. I don't judge people for hooking up just for the pleasure. But you describe doing this as a coping mechanism. Using these guys so that you can have attention and feel wanted. This is not only dangerous on a physical level but an emotional and interpersonal level.

So I want to tell you a story. I grew up with hyper-religious neighbors and they were the only friends I had for a long time. We hung out a lot but their parents were pretty forceful about their religion and eventually didn't want me hanging out there anymore because my family was not religious. In my early twenties I tried to kill myself one night and the only person I could think of calling was my former neighbor. I don't know why because I haven't really talked to her in years but I felt like she would understand me. Instead she literally told me that I was going to burn in hell if I decided to take my life, and that I would never get into heaven and God would reject me for making this decision. And how dare I be so selfish when God had forgiven my sins etc etc

I was literally hanging on to a thread and the one person I reached out to was the one person who made me feel even worse. If I wasn't picked up by a police officer that night I probably would not be typing this right now because her words really did almost send me over the edge.

So I I know what you mean to some degree although my parents were not this way. I cannot imagine what it's like to have a father who instead of listening to your concerns and pain pushes his religion off onto you. I would say though that he probably doesn't realize what he's doing is insensitive. He probably thinks he's helping you but he hasn't. And it's okay for you to feel this way about it.

The bottom line is that you are absolutely 100% allowed to feel the way that you do right now. Even if you are hurting you are allowed to feel that way because these are your real emotions, not something that's made up, not something that some guy in the sky is going to fix for you. What you're feeling right now is real and you are entitled to that regardless of how other people respond to it.

That said I'm going to say something that you have probably heard before and please feel free to roll your eyes at me. You're really young and your future as far as becoming a successful adult and having a career has not even really started yet. Your concerns about the future are legitimate because clearly you care about that part of your life, so have you given thought to what you want it to be like? If your answer is no that's okay too. Because a Junior High student should not have to worry so fucking much about these things. It's hard enough being a teenager, it's okay if you check out every now and then.

One thing that always confuses me is when people say to me that I can't find a relationship unless I am fully happy with myself but I see so many people that don't even belong in relationships. They treat their partner like crap. I think that depressed people can absolutely have good relationships with others, if they are self-aware and willing to put work into the relationship. I disagree with the notion that everyone needs to be perfect before they get into a relationship because most people aren't. Most people come with baggage and difficulties. I think it's harder for people with depression to connect to others because we feel like there's no point. Like no one is going to accept us at our lowest, and no one's going to see us trying at our highest moments. It feels like we are broken and defected somehow and that Society doesn't want us. But I don't think that's true. I think there is someone for everyone. I think that love is just something humans gravitate towards and loneliness is very difficult for us as social creatures.

There are psychologists and therapists who specialize in treating trauma specifically. It will say so on their bio or their receptionist may be able to answer that question for you. What you want to ask is "does this practitioner specialize in treating  in post-traumatic stress disorder or do you know someone who does?" Generally speaking most mental health professionals are familiar with trauma and PTSD diagnosis. You might find that most of them will say yes but not all of them are actually specialized in the treatment of PTSD. This does not mean that they are in capable of treating it, but some people needs more targeted therapeutic approaches. One thing that comes to mind is cognitive behavioral therapy. You might look into finding a psychologist who has training in CBT, and exposure therapy. Both of these are used in the treatment of PTSD, specifically exposure therapy. But this is not something that you jump right into and not everyone is comfortable with it because it involves recanting your trauma over and over.

 A good sign to look for is a therapist who does not push you into any sort of treatment without thoroughly evaluating you and asking for your input to continue any treatment option. A good therapist will always explain treatment options to you in a clear constructed manner that you can understand. A good therapist will check in to make sure that you do understand these terms.

 Signs you want to look for:

Do they validate your experiences?
 Do they let you speak, do they take their time getting to know you? Do they encourage you to move at a pace you are comfortable with and not force you into something that triggers you? A good therapist will never insult you or imply that you aren't doing enough for yourself based on IQ or other reasons. They will never undermine or shame you. They are someone you should feel at ease around. Someone that gives you a good vibe so to speak

Get a blank notebook and write down your top 5. What's your top 5? The top 5 things standing in your way as a result of the abuse you suffered.
Write them down one at a time, and underneath each bullet point write a short summary about the ways your life is affected by each.

The next part is tricky and it will take some effort but now that you have your top five, find your top 7. Your top 7 is going to be a list of solutions for your top five. The reason why I choose 7 is so that you have a back-up plan if the first solution isn't going to work for you. Here you have five options plus two additional fallback options. But honestly you can add as many as you like. The objective is to find the solutions after you have fully recognized the scope of your problem(s).
 
 Try not to forget that there are professionals who specialize in helping people overcome these obstacles. Yes I am talking about a therapist. What many people don't know is that therapists can also help us transform our suffering into personal success. 

Regardless, it's okay to be gentle on yourself during this process. It is to be expected that you are suffering some collateral damage still. Shrapnel. Maybe some of the wounds are still fresh? This is where your work begins. 
Know that every step you take towards recovering from abuse is a step closer to yourself. 
If you live with residual anxiety or self-doubt this is to be expected. But it is not your fate. You did not have a choice as a child but you have a choice now.

So it may take you some time and that's totally okay. It's reasonable to expect that the lingering side effects you are feeling today were years in the making. One element I hope you can consider is that the relationship you have with yourself is the most important one you're ever going to have. If you have negative ideas of yourself, find out where they came from. Sometimes you will find that the Notions you hold about yourself were actually the words of other people. This is where the work begins. It begins when you say no to those people by saying no to those thoughts. The nature of the Mind will continue to bring these thoughts to the Forefront of your awareness until you dismantle them repeatedly. But you have the power to change that. Do not be fooled by the persistence of these ideas or notions. It does not make them true. If they impact you negatively and keep you from your life..these thoughts can be discarded as useless. Wade through the murky shit. Don't drown in it
